experiments.title: The Rice Test: how much rice is one lakh grains?
experiments.context: In this test you count out one thousand grains of rice. Then you build ten thousand and one lakh, each time by taking ten of the amount before.
experiments.question: How much space do one lakh grains of rice take: a spoon, a tumbler, a cooking pot, a bucket or a whole room?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess: would one lakh grains of rice fill a spoon, a tumbler, a cooking pot, a bucket or a room? Say why you think so. Write your guess down.
experiments.fair_test: We use the same rice all the way through. We count the first thousand grains one by one. After that, each new amount is ten of the amount before, measured with the same spoon or the same tumbler filled to the same mark. So only the first thousand is an exact count. The bigger amounts are close, not exact.

materials.item: raw rice from your rice tin (all of it goes back afterwards)
a large, clean, dry steel plate
a tablespoon, or a small bottle cap or tiny katori
a steel tumbler or a cup
a large pot that holds 4 litres or more, or a clean dry bucket
a rubber band or a marker, to mark a level on the tumbler
paper and a pencil

experiments.safety: Wash and dry your hands first, because the rice goes back in the tin. Keep raw rice away from babies and toddlers, who could choke on it.

schedule.what: Count a thousand grains of rice, then build ten thousand and one lakh in steps of ten, and compare with your guess.

experiments.record: Draw the table with four columns. Fill one row for each amount: 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 and 1,00,000. Under the table write three lines: what I think, what I saw, and why.

example_chart.title: What a finished table can look like (your rice and your spoon will give your own answers)
rows: a small square patch on the plate
2 to 3 litres, about half a large pot

setup.art: A steel plate with rice grains arranged in ten neat rows of ten, and a child's finger sliding the last grain into place.
setup.caption: 1. Make ten rows of ten grains. That is a hundred.

setup.art: Ten small heaps of rice on a steel plate being pushed together into one heap, with a tablespoon waiting beside the plate.
setup.caption: 2. Make ten heaps of a hundred. Push them together. That is a thousand.

setup.art: A tablespoon of rice being tipped into a steel tumbler that has a rubber band around it to mark a level.
setup.caption: 3. Ten spoonfuls of a thousand go into the tumbler. That is ten thousand.

setup.art: A steel tumbler of rice being poured into a large cooking pot that is about half full of rice.
setup.caption: 4. Ten tumblers go into the pot. That is one lakh.

flow.do: 1. Put the spoon, the tumbler, the pot and a bucket in a row. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Imagine one lakh grains of rice. Would they fill this spoon, this tumbler, this pot, this bucket, or the room? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Think of one lakh grains of rice. Would they fill a spoon, a tumbler or a pot? Or a bucket, or a room? Say why. Write your guess.

ask.q: What makes you think that?
good: A lakh is a huge number, so it must be a room.
Rice grains are tiny, so maybe a bucket.
Any guess that comes with a reason.

flow.parent: Do not hint. Most children and many adults guess far too big. Write the guess where everyone can see it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Rice Test, where you build one lakh grains of rice in steps of ten. You guess before you count.

flow.do: 1. Tip a small handful of rice on the plate. 2. Your child slides out ten grains into a row. 3. Then nine more rows of ten under it.
flow.say: Make a row of ten grains. Now make ten rows like that. How many grains are in the square?
flow.kid: Slide ten grains into a row. Make ten rows. How many grains is that?

ask.q: How do you know it is a hundred without counting every grain again?
good: Ten rows of ten is a hundred.
10 times 10 is 100.

flow.parent: Broken grains count as grains. The rows do not need to be neat, only complete.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Rice Test, where you build one lakh grains of rice in steps of ten. You make a square of one hundred grains.

flow.do: 1. Push the hundred into a heap at the edge of the plate. 2. You and your child each make more heaps of a hundred. 3. Stop when there are ten heaps. 4. Push the ten heaps together.
flow.say: We need ten heaps of a hundred. You make some and I will make some. What will ten hundreds come to?
flow.kid: Make more heaps of a hundred. A grown-up can help. Stop at ten heaps. Push them together.
flow.parent: This is the slow part, and it matters. Your child feels how much work a thousand is. Share the counting so it takes about eight minutes.

check.q: Ten heaps of one hundred grains are pushed together. How many grains is that?
check.why: Ten hundreds make one thousand. Picking 110 means adding ten to a hundred, when the step is ten times a hundred.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the Rice Test, where you build one lakh grains of rice in steps of ten. You make ten heaps of a hundred, which is one thousand grains.

flow.do: 1. Scoop the thousand grains into the tablespoon. 2. See how full the spoon is. 3. If they do not fit, use a bottle cap or tiny katori that they just fill.
flow.say: This spoonful is one thousand grains. Look hard at how full it is. From now on this spoon is our thousand.
flow.kid: Scoop your thousand grains into the spoon. Look how full it is. This spoonful is your thousand.

ask.q: Is a thousand grains more or less than you expected?
good: Less. It is only a spoonful.
It looked like more on the plate.

flow.parent: For most rice, a thousand grains come to about one tablespoon. Fat grains such as idli rice can need nearly two. Remember exactly how full the spoon was.
flow.context: This is step 4 of the Rice Test, where you build one lakh grains of rice in steps of ten. You find a spoon that one thousand grains fill.

flow.do: 1. Ask how full the tumbler will be with ten thousand grains. 2. Your child puts ten spoonfuls into the tumbler, each as full as the first. 3. Mark the level with the rubber band.
flow.say: Ten of these spoonfuls make ten thousand. Guess first: how full will the tumbler be? Now count the spoonfuls aloud.
flow.kid: Guess how full the tumbler will get. Put in ten spoonfuls. Count them aloud. Mark the level.
flow.parent: Ten thousand grains usually come to about one tumbler. If your tumbler overflows, use a bigger cup. The mark is now your ten thousand.
flow.context: This is step 5 of the Rice Test, where you build one lakh grains of rice in steps of ten. Ten spoonfuls of a thousand grains make ten thousand in the tumbler.

flow.do: 1. Tip the tumbler into the big pot. 2. Fill the tumbler to the mark from the rice tin and tip it in again. 3. Do this until ten tumblers are in the pot. 4. Put the pot beside the first guess.
flow.say: Ten tumblers of ten thousand make one lakh. Count the tumblers aloud. Now look at the pot. How does it compare with your guess?
flow.kid: Pour ten tumblers into the pot. Fill each to the mark. Count them aloud. That is one lakh grains. Look at your guess.

ask.q: Was your guess too big, too small or about right?
good: Too big. I said a room and it is only a pot.
About right.

flow.parent: If you have less rice, pour three tumblers and ask your child how high ten would come. One lakh grains usually weigh between 1 and 2.5 kg.
flow.context: This is step 6 of the Rice Test, where you build one lakh grains of rice in steps of ten. Ten tumblers of ten thousand grains make one lakh in the pot.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the table together. 2. Ask the two questions below, and wait for your child's own words. 3. Your child writes three lines: what I think, what I saw, and why. 4. Pour the rice back into the tin.
flow.say: What did we do at every step to get the next amount? What would ten of these pots be called?
flow.kid: Fill in your table. What did you do at every step? Write what you think, what you saw, and why.

ask.q: What did we do at every step?
good: We took ten of the one before.
Ten times, every time.

ask.q: What would ten pots like this hold?
good: Ten lakh.
Ten lakh grains, which is one million.

flow.parent: A strong answer: 'One lakh grains fill a pot. I saw that each step was ten of the step before. So a lakh is ten times ten times a thousand.' Ten pots would be ten lakh grains, about one large sack of rice.

check.q: In the Rice Test, how was each new amount made from the one before?
options: By taking ten of the amount before
check.why: Each amount was ten of the one before: ten hundreds, ten thousands, ten ten-thousands. Picking 'adding ten' mixes up ten more with ten times.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Rice Test, where you build one lakh grains of rice in steps of ten. You fill in the table and say what rule you found.

activities.title: Two Commas, One Number
activities.context: In this activity you write a long number on a strip of paper and use dried beans as commas. You read it the Indian way, then move the beans and read it the international way.
activities.problem: Does a number change when its commas move?

materials.item: a strip of paper about as long as your forearm
dried beans, chana or bindis to use as commas
a pencil or sketch pen

schedule.what: Write a seven-digit number on a strip, place bean commas the Indian way and the international way, and read it both ways.

activities.record: Draw the strip twice in your notebook, once with Indian commas and once with international commas. Write the number in words under each. Then write: 1 lakh = 100 thousand, and 10 lakh = 1 million.

setup.art: A paper strip with the digits 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 written with even gaps, and two beans placed in the gaps to read 34,56,789.
setup.caption: 1. Write seven digits. Put beans as commas the Indian way: after three digits from the right, then after two.

setup.art: The same paper strip with the beans moved to read 3,456,789, and a child's hand sliding one bean.
setup.caption: 2. Move the beans: one after every three digits. Read the number again.

setup.art: A notebook page with both versions written out and an equals sign between them.
setup.caption: 3. Write both ways down. The digits are the same.

flow.do: 1. Your child writes 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 on the strip, with a finger-width gap between digits. 2. Ask the question below before any bean is placed.
flow.say: We will put commas in this number in two different ways. Will the number itself change? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Write 3 4 5 6 7 8 9 on the strip. Leave gaps. Guess: if the commas move, does the number change?

ask.q: Will the number change when the commas move?
good: No, the digits stay where they are.
Yes, because the groups are different.
Any answer with a reason.

flow.context: This is the first step of Two Commas, One Number, where you move bean commas along a strip of digits. You write the digits and guess what moving the commas will do.

flow.do: 1. Your child counts three digits from the right and puts a bean there. 2. Then two more digits, and another bean. 3. Your child reads the number aloud.
flow.say: Start from the right. Three digits, then a comma. Two digits, then a comma. Now read it to me in lakhs.
flow.kid: Count three digits from the right. Put a bean. Count two more. Put a bean. Read the number in lakhs.

ask.q: What does the strip say?
good: Thirty-four lakh fifty-six thousand seven hundred eighty-nine.

flow.parent: The strip should read 34,56,789. If your child starts from the left, ask which end the ones place is at.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Two Commas, One Number, where you move bean commas along a strip of digits. You place the commas the Indian way and read the number.

flow.do: 1. Your child takes the beans off. 2. Now a bean goes after every three digits from the right. 3. Your child reads the number aloud in millions.
flow.say: Now do it the international way. A comma after every three digits from the right. Read it in millions and thousands.
flow.kid: Take the beans off. Put a bean after every three digits, from the right. Read the number in millions.

ask.q: What does the strip say now?
good: Three million four hundred fifty-six thousand seven hundred eighty-nine.

ask.q: Did any digit move?
good: No. Only the beans moved.

check.why: They are the same number. The digits are the same and stand in the same places. Only the commas moved. Picking the first usually means reading '34' as bigger than '3' without looking at the places.

flow.context: This is step 3 of Two Commas, One Number, where you move bean commas along a strip of digits. You move the commas to the international way and read the number again.

flow.do: 1. On the second strip your child writes 1 0 0 0 0 0. 2. Place commas both ways and read both. 3. Add one more zero and do it again. 4. Your child writes the two facts in the notebook.
flow.say: Write one lakh. Read it the international way. Now add a zero. What is it called in each system?
flow.kid: Write one lakh on a new strip. Read it both ways. Add one more zero. Read it both ways again.

ask.q: What is one lakh called in the international system?
good: One hundred thousand.

ask.q: What is ten lakh called?
good: One million.

flow.parent: The two facts to keep: 1 lakh is 100 thousand, and 10 lakh is 1 million.
flow.context: This is the last step of Two Commas, One Number, where you move bean commas along a strip of digits. You find what one lakh and ten lakh are called in the international system.

activities.title: A Lakh on a String: the millimetre number line
activities.context: In this activity you start with one millimetre on a ruler and make each new length ten times the one before, until you know how long one lakh millimetres is.
activities.problem: How long is a line of one lakh millimetres? Would it fit in your home?

materials.item: a ruler marked in millimetres
string or wool, a little over 1 metre
small slips of paper and a pencil
scissors

schedule.what: Build 1, 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 millimetres with a ruler and string, then work out one lakh millimetres.

activities.record: Draw a number line from 0 to 1,00,000 across your notebook page, with a mark at every 10,000. Put a dot where 1,000 would be. Write how long each length was in millimetres and in metres.

setup.art: A ruler lying on paper with pencil marks at 1 mm, 10 mm and 100 mm, each labelled.
setup.caption: 1. Mark 1 mm, 10 mm and 100 mm with the ruler.

setup.art: A child cutting a piece of string held against ten ruler-lengths of 100 mm marked on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Ten lots of 100 mm make 1,000 mm. Cut a string that long. It is 1 metre.

setup.art: A child laying the same string end to end along a corridor floor, with paper slips marking each length.
setup.caption: 3. Lay the string ten times, end to end. That is 10,000 mm.

flow.do: 1. Show one millimetre on the ruler. 2. Ask the question below and write the guess.
flow.say: This tiny gap is one millimetre. How long would one lakh of them be, laid end to end? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Find one millimetre on the ruler. Guess how long one lakh millimetres would be. Say why.

ask.q: Would it fit in this room? In this street?
good: Any guess with a reason.

flow.context: This is the first step of A Lakh on a String, where you build a line of one lakh millimetres. You guess how long one lakh millimetres is.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a line 1 mm long, then 10 mm, then 100 mm. 2. Label each one. 3. Ask how each was made from the one before.
flow.say: Draw one millimetre. Now ten times that. Now ten times that again. What are the three lengths?
flow.kid: Draw a line 1 mm long. Then 10 mm. Then 100 mm. Write the length beside each.
flow.parent: 10 mm is 1 centimetre and 100 mm is 10 centimetres. Let your child notice this.
flow.context: This is step 2 of A Lakh on a String, where you build a line of one lakh millimetres. You draw the first three lengths, each ten times the one before.

flow.do: 1. Mark ten lengths of 100 mm in a line on the floor. 2. Cut the string to match the whole line. 3. Check it against a metre tape if you have one.
flow.say: Ten of the 100 millimetre lengths make the next step. How many millimetres is that? Cut the string to fit.
flow.kid: Mark ten lengths of 100 mm on the floor. Cut a string that long. How many millimetres is it?
flow.parent: The string should be 1 metre long. A grown-up should help with the scissors.
flow.context: This is step 3 of A Lakh on a String, where you build a line of one lakh millimetres. You make a string of one thousand millimetres, which is one metre.

flow.do: 1. Start at one wall. 2. Lay the string end to end ten times, putting a slip at each end point. 3. Turn a corner if the room is too short.
flow.say: Ten strings make the next step. Count the strings as you go. How many millimetres have we laid now?
flow.kid: Lay your string ten times, end to end. Mark each end with a slip. Count as you go.

check.q: 1,000 mm is 1 metre. How long is 10,000 mm?
check.why: Ten times 1 metre is 10 metres. Picking 100 metres means taking two steps of ten when only one was taken.

flow.context: This is step 4 of A Lakh on a String, where you build a line of one lakh millimetres. You lay the metre string ten times to make ten thousand millimetres.

flow.do: 1. Ask how long ten of these 10 metre lines would be. 2. Name a place about 100 metres from your door. 3. Your child draws the number line in the notebook.
flow.say: One more step of ten gives one lakh millimetres. How many metres is that? What is about that far from our door?
flow.kid: Ten lines of 10 metres make one lakh millimetres. How many metres is that? Draw your number line.

ask.q: How long is one lakh millimetres?
good: 100 metres.

ask.q: And ten lakh millimetres?
good: 1,000 metres, which is 1 kilometre.

flow.parent: On the notebook number line from 0 to 1,00,000, the dot for 1,000 sits almost on top of zero. That surprises most children. Let them find it.
flow.context: This is the last step of A Lakh on a String, where you build a line of one lakh millimetres. You work out that one lakh millimetres is 100 metres.

activities.title: Maths in life: the Big-Number Hunt in the market and on the screen
activities.context: In this activity the family collects real big numbers from newspaper advertisements, shop boards and a phone. You write each one in a place value chart and say it in both systems.
activities.problem: Markets in India talk in lakhs. Phones and websites talk in K and M. Can you read both and tell which number is bigger?

materials.item: a newspaper with advertisements for flats, vehicles or jewellery
a phone, used with a grown-up
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Collect six real big numbers, write them in a place value chart, change K and M into lakhs, and put them in order.

activities.record: Make a table with four columns: where we found it, how it was written, the number with Indian commas, the number in words. Fill one row for each of your six numbers.

setup.art: A newspaper page of property and scooter advertisements with three prices circled in pencil, such as ₹45 lakh and ₹1,12,000.
setup.caption: 1. Circle big prices in a newspaper or on shop boards.

setup.art: A phone screen showing a list of videos with view counts such as 250K and 1.2M, and a child copying them onto paper.
setup.caption: 2. With a grown-up, copy big numbers from a phone: views, followers, downloads.

setup.art: A hand-drawn place value chart with seven columns and six different numbers written in its rows.
setup.caption: 3. Write every number in a place value chart. Then put them in order.

flow.do: 1. Find three prices above ₹50,000 in the newspaper or on shop boards. 2. With your child, find three counts on a phone that use K or M. 3. Your child copies each one exactly as written.
flow.say: Let us hunt for big numbers. Find three in the paper and three on the phone. Copy each one just as it is printed.
flow.kid: Find three big prices in the paper. Find three big numbers on a phone with a grown-up. Copy them exactly.
flow.parent: Good places to look: flat and plot prices, scooters and cars, gold jewellery, and view counts under videos. Stay with your child while the phone is in use.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Big-Number Hunt, where you collect real numbers from the market and the screen. You collect six real numbers.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a place value chart with seven columns, from ten lakhs to ones. 2. Each newspaper number goes in one row, one digit to a column.
flow.say: Write each price in the chart, one digit in each column. Start from the ones. What is '45 lakh' in figures?
flow.kid: Draw a chart with seven columns. Write each price in it. Put one digit in each column.

ask.q: How do you write 45 lakh in figures?
good: A 4 in ten lakhs, a 5 in lakhs and five zeros.

flow.parent: A price in crores will not fit in seven columns. Add a column on the left, or choose another number.
flow.context: This is step 2 of the Big-Number Hunt, where you collect real numbers from the market and the screen. You write the newspaper prices in a place value chart.

flow.do: 1. Take the phone numbers one by one. 2. For K, write the number and then three zeros. 3. For M, move to the millions column. 4. Put Indian commas and read each in lakhs.
flow.say: K means thousand and M means million. So what is 250K in figures? And how many lakh is 1.2M?
flow.kid: K means thousand. M means million. Write each phone number in the chart. Read it in lakhs.

ask.q: How many lakh is 1.2M?
good: 12 lakh.
One million is ten lakh, and 0.2 million is two lakh.

check.q: A video has 250K views. How is that written with Indian commas?
check.why: 250K is 250 thousand, which is 2,50,000, or two and a half lakh. Picking 25,00,000 treats K as ten thousand.

flow.context: This is step 3 of the Big-Number Hunt, where you collect real numbers from the market and the screen. You change numbers written with K and M into lakhs.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts all six numbers in order, smallest first. 2. Ask who each number was written for.
flow.say: Put the six numbers in order. Then tell me: why did the newspaper use lakhs and the phone use M?
flow.kid: Put your six numbers in order, smallest first. Why did the paper say lakh and the phone say M?

ask.q: Why did the newspaper use lakhs and the phone use M?
good: The newspaper is for readers in India.
The app is made for people all over the world.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Big-Number Hunt, where you collect real numbers from the market and the screen. You order the numbers and think about who each was written for.

activities.title: Maths in life: Bundles at the Bank
activities.context: In this activity you make one lakh rupees out of paper notes in different ways. Banks tie notes into packets of 100, and you do the same.
activities.problem: How many notes make one lakh rupees? It depends on the note, and place value gives the answer without long sums.

materials.item: small slips of paper to stand for packets of notes
a pencil
real notes of ₹10, ₹100 and ₹500 to look at, if you have them

schedule.what: Work out how many ₹500, ₹100 and ₹10 notes make one lakh rupees, and how many bank packets that is.

activities.record: Make a table with three columns: the note, how many notes make ₹1,00,000, and how many packets of 100 that is. Fill in rows for ₹500, ₹100 and ₹10.

setup.art: Paper slips on a table, each marked '100 notes of ₹500', being laid out in a row by a child.
setup.caption: 1. One slip stands for one bank packet: 100 notes.

setup.art: Two slips marked ₹500 packets beside ten slips marked ₹100 packets, with ₹1,00,000 written above each group.
setup.caption: 2. Make one lakh rupees with ₹500 packets, then with ₹100 packets.

setup.art: A notebook table with three rows for ₹500, ₹100 and ₹10 notes and the number of notes and packets filled in.
setup.caption: 3. Write what you found. Look for the pattern.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that a bank packet holds 100 notes. 2. Your child marks one slip '100 notes of ₹100'. 3. Ask what one packet is worth.
flow.say: A bank ties 100 notes into a packet. What is a packet of ₹100 notes worth? How do you know?
flow.kid: A bank packet has 100 notes. What is a packet of ₹100 notes worth? Mark a slip for it.

ask.q: What is 100 × 100?
good: The 1 moves two places to the left, so ten thousand.

flow.context: This is the first step of Bundles at the Bank, where you make one lakh rupees from paper notes. You find what one packet of notes is worth.

flow.do: 1. Your child lays out packets of ₹100 notes until they make one lakh. 2. Count the packets. 3. Work out the number of notes.
flow.say: Each packet is ten thousand rupees. How many packets make one lakh? So how many ₹100 notes is that?
flow.kid: Lay out packets of ₹100 notes. Stop at one lakh rupees. How many packets? How many notes?

ask.q: How many ₹100 notes make one lakh rupees?
good: 1,000 notes.
Ten packets of 100 notes.

check.why: One lakh divided by 100 is 1,000. Every digit moves two places to the right. Picking 100 would give only ten thousand rupees.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Bundles at the Bank, where you make one lakh rupees from paper notes. You make one lakh rupees from ₹100 notes.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess: will ₹10 notes need more notes or fewer? 2. Your child works it out. 3. Then do the same for ₹500 notes.
flow.say: A ₹10 note is ten times smaller than a ₹100 note. So how many ₹10 notes make one lakh? And how many ₹500 notes?
flow.kid: Now use ₹10 notes. How many make one lakh rupees? Then try ₹500 notes.

ask.q: How many ₹10 notes make one lakh rupees?
good: 10,000 notes, which is 100 packets.

ask.q: How many ₹500 notes?
good: 200 notes, which is 2 packets.

flow.parent: One lakh divided by 500 is harder. A good way: two ₹500 notes make a thousand, and a lakh is a hundred thousands, so 200 notes.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Bundles at the Bank, where you make one lakh rupees from paper notes. You make one lakh rupees from ₹10 notes and from ₹500 notes.

flow.do: 1. Your child fills in the table. 2. Ask what happens to the number of notes when the note is ten times smaller.
flow.say: Look at the ₹100 row and the ₹10 row. The note became ten times smaller. What happened to the number of notes?
flow.kid: Fill in your table. The note got ten times smaller. What happened to the number of notes?

ask.q: What is the pattern?
good: Ten times smaller note, ten times as many notes.
The digits moved one place to the left.

flow.context: This is the last step of Bundles at the Bank, where you make one lakh rupees from paper notes. You look for the pattern in your table.

activities.title: Everyone does maths: Walk Like a Desert Ant
activities.context: Desert ants find their way home by keeping track of their own steps. In this activity you try it yourself, with your eyes closed, first with normal steps and then with giant steps.
activities.problem: If you measure a distance by your steps, what happens when your steps change size?

materials.item: the longest clear stretch of floor in your home, about 6 metres
a cushion to mark the nest
10 dried beans in a pocket, to keep count in tens

activities.safety: Clear the floor first. A grown-up walks beside the child whenever the child's eyes are closed.

schedule.what: Walk a counted number of steps away from a cushion, then walk back with eyes closed, first with normal steps and then with giant steps.

activities.record: Draw the corridor. Mark the cushion, where you stopped with normal steps, and where you stopped with giant steps. Write one line saying why they differ.

setup.art: A child standing beside a cushion at one end of a corridor, about to walk away from it, with a grown-up watching.
setup.caption: 1. The cushion is the nest. Put it in the middle. Walk away and count your steps.

setup.art: The same child walking back along the corridor with eyes closed, a grown-up walking close beside.
setup.caption: 2. Turn round. Close your eyes. Walk back the same number of steps.

setup.art: The child taking very long strides with eyes closed and going well past the cushion.
setup.caption: 3. Do it again with giant steps. Where do you stop now?

flow.do: 1. Put the cushion in the middle of the clear stretch. 2. Your child walks 6 normal steps away, counting aloud. 3. Your child turns, closes both eyes and walks 6 steps back. 4. Walk beside your child.
flow.say: The cushion is your nest. Walk six steps away. Now close your eyes and walk six steps back. Where is the nest?
flow.kid: Walk 6 steps away from the cushion. Turn round. Close your eyes. Walk 6 steps back.

ask.q: How close to the cushion did you stop?
good: Very close.
Just beside it.

flow.context: This is the first step of Walk Like a Desert Ant, where you find your way back by counting steps. You walk away from the cushion and find it again by counting steps.

flow.do: 1. Ask for a guess: what will happen with giant steps on the way back? 2. Your child walks 6 normal steps away again. 3. Your child comes back with eyes closed, taking 6 giant steps.
flow.say: This time walk out normally but come back with giant steps. Where will you end up? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess first. Walk 6 normal steps away. Come back with 6 giant steps, eyes closed. Where are you?

ask.q: Where did you stop, and why?
good: Past the cushion, because each step was longer.
Too far. Same number of steps but bigger steps.

flow.parent: Read this aloud only after the walk. In 2006 scientists gave desert ants longer legs with tiny stilts. Those ants walked past their nest in the same way.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Walk Like a Desert Ant, where you find your way back by counting steps. You come back with giant steps and see where you stop.

flow.do: 1. Give your child 10 beans in one pocket. 2. Your child walks round the home for 100 steps. 3. After every ten steps, one bean moves to the other pocket.
flow.say: Now a long count. Walk a hundred steps. Move one bean to your other pocket after every ten steps.
flow.kid: Walk 100 steps. After every ten steps, move one bean to your other pocket.

ask.q: How did the beans help?
good: I only had to count to ten each time.
Each bean stood for ten steps.

check.q: You moved 7 beans and then took 4 more steps. How many steps is that?
check.why: Each bean stands for ten steps. Seven beans are 70 steps, and 4 more make 74. Picking 11 counts a bean as one step. A bean in the other pocket is worth ten, just as a digit in the tens place is.

flow.context: This is the last step of Walk Like a Desert Ant, where you find your way back by counting steps. You keep a long count by moving one bean for every ten steps.

games.title: Place It! The biggest number wins
games.players: 1 to 3 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a card game. You turn over digits one at a time and must decide at once which place to put each one in. The biggest six-digit number wins.

printables.title: A place value mat with six boxes in a row (draw one for each player)
20 digit cards: two each of the digits 0 to 9

rules: Each player draws a mat: six boxes in a row, named Lakhs, Ten thousands, Thousands, Hundreds, Tens and Ones. Shuffle the 20 digit cards and put them face down.
On your turn, turn over the top card. Write that digit in any empty box on your mat. Once a digit is written, it can not be moved. Put the card aside.
Take turns until every box is full. That is six turns each.
Each player reads their number aloud the Indian way. The biggest number wins the round and scores 1 point.
The winner scores 1 more point for reading the number the international way as well.
Shuffle all 20 cards again for the next round. The first player to reach 5 points wins the game.
Playing alone: play three rounds and try to beat your own biggest number. Or choose a target, such as 5,00,000, and try to land as close to it as you can.

setup.art: Two hand-drawn mats of six boxes labelled from Lakhs to Ones, and a face-down pile of small paper digit cards between them.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a mat each. Shuffle the 20 digit cards.

setup.art: A child holding a card showing 9 above her mat, about to write it in the Lakhs box.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over a card. Choose a box for that digit. It stays there.

setup.art: Two filled mats reading 9,75,310 and 8,64,201, with the first one ticked.
setup.caption: 3. Read your numbers aloud. The biggest wins.

flow.do: 1. Cut 20 small paper cards and write the digits 0 to 9 twice. 2. Each player draws a mat of six boxes with the place names under them. 3. Shuffle the cards face down.
flow.say: This game is about where you put each digit. Once you write a digit in a box, it stays there.
flow.kid: Make 20 digit cards. Draw a mat with six boxes. Write the place names under the boxes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Place It, a card game where you build the biggest six-digit number. You make the cards and the mats.

flow.do: 1. Play one practice round with the mats face up, talking about each choice. 2. Ask where a 9 should go, and where a 0 should go.
flow.say: Suppose you turn over a 9 first. Which box will you put it in? What about a 0?
flow.kid: Play a practice round. If you turn over a 9, which box is best? What about a 0?

check.q: You want the biggest number. Your first card is a 9. Which box is best?
check.why: The lakhs place is worth the most, so a 9 there adds nine lakh. In the ones place it adds only nine.

flow.parent: The hard choices are the middle digits. A 5 on the first turn has no safe box. Let your child feel that and choose.
flow.context: This is step 2 of Place It, a card game where you build the biggest six-digit number. You play a practice round and talk about where to put high and low digits.

flow.do: 1. Play rounds until someone has 5 points. 2. After each round, each player reads their number aloud in the Indian way. 3. The winner reads it the international way for the extra point.
flow.say: Read your number to me in lakhs. Now, for one more point, read it the international way.
flow.kid: Play the game. Read your number in lakhs each round. Read it the international way for an extra point.
flow.parent: A zero in the lakhs box makes a five-digit number. That is allowed, and it is a good thing to talk about.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Place It, a card game where you build the biggest six-digit number. You play the game to 5 points.

flow.do: 1. Ask the two questions below. 2. Then play one round where the smallest number wins.
flow.say: Where did you put your low digits, and why? What changes when the smallest number wins?
flow.kid: Where did you put your low digits? Why? Now play one round where the smallest number wins.

ask.q: Where do low digits belong when you want a big number?
good: On the right, where they cost the least.
In the ones and tens.

flow.context: This is the last step of Place It, a card game where you build the biggest six-digit number. You say what your plan was, and try the game the other way round.

games.title: Lakh and Million Pairs
games.players: 1 to 4 players: alone, with a parent or with friends
games.context: This is a memory game with 24 cards. Twelve cards show a number with Indian commas. Twelve show the same numbers the international way. You find the two cards that are the same number.

printables.title: 24 cards: 12 numbers with Indian commas and the same 12 numbers the international way
items: 999,999 (nine hundred ninety-nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine)

rules: Copy the 24 cards onto slips of paper, one number to a slip. Shuffle them and lay them face down in four rows of six.
On your turn, turn over two cards. If they show the same number, read both cards aloud: one in lakhs, one in thousands or millions. Then keep the pair and take another turn.
If the two cards do not show the same number, turn them face down again in the same spots. The next player takes a turn.
To check a pair, cover the commas with your finger. A true pair has the same digits in the same order.
Watch out for 1,20,000 and 12,00,000. They look alike, but they are different numbers.
When all the cards are taken, the player with the most pairs wins.
Playing alone: count how many turns you need to clear all 12 pairs. Play again and try to need fewer.

setup.art: Twenty-four small paper slips laid face down in four rows of six on a floor mat.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the 24 cards face down in four rows of six.

setup.art: Two cards turned face up showing 2,50,000 and 250,000 (two hundred fifty thousand), with a child pointing at both.
setup.caption: 2. Turn over two cards. Same number? Read both aloud and keep them.

setup.art: A finger covering the commas on the cards 12,00,000 and 1,200,000 to show the same seven digits underneath.
setup.caption: 3. Not sure? Cover the commas and compare the digits.

flow.do: 1. Copy the 24 cards onto paper slips. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Lay them face down in four rows of six.
flow.say: Half of these cards use Indian commas. The other half show the same numbers the international way.
flow.kid: Copy the 24 cards onto slips. Shuffle them. Lay them face down in four rows.
flow.context: This is the first step of Lakh and Million Pairs, a memory game with numbers written in two systems. You make the cards and lay them out.

flow.do: 1. Turn two cards face up as an example: 2,50,000 and 250,000. 2. Show how to check by covering the commas. 3. Read both aloud.
flow.say: Are these two the same number? Cover the commas and look at the digits. Now read each card aloud.
flow.kid: Look at the two cards. Cover the commas. Are the digits the same? Read both cards aloud.

check.q: Which card is a pair for 12,00,000?
check.why: Take out the commas: 12,00,000 is 1200000, which has seven digits. Only 1,200,000 has the same seven digits. 120,000 has six digits, so it is one lakh twenty thousand.

flow.context: This is step 2 of Lakh and Million Pairs, a memory game with numbers written in two systems. You learn how to check whether two cards are a pair.

flow.do: 1. Play the game. 2. Each time a pair is found, the player reads both cards aloud before keeping them.
flow.say: Read both cards before you take them. One in lakhs, and one in thousands or millions.
flow.kid: Play the game. When you find a pair, read both cards aloud. Then keep them.
flow.parent: If a player cannot read a card, read it together. The reading aloud is where the learning happens.
flow.context: This is step 3 of Lakh and Million Pairs, a memory game with numbers written in two systems. You play until all the pairs are found.

flow.do: 1. Lay out the pairs you won. 2. Ask which pair was hardest to spot, and why.
flow.say: Which pair was hardest to spot? What did you look at to be sure?
flow.kid: Lay out your pairs. Which one was hardest to spot? How did you make sure?

ask.q: What did you look at to be sure of a pair?
good: The number of digits.
The digits without the commas.

flow.context: This is the last step of Lakh and Million Pairs, a memory game with numbers written in two systems. You talk about how you told the pairs apart.

projects.title: Meter Watch: five days with a machine that counts in places
projects.context: In this five-day project you read the same meter once a day. It can be the electricity meter of your home or the kilometre counter of a scooter or car. You watch the digits roll from place to place.
projects.problem: A meter shows a row of digits. Which digit changes most often, and when does the digit on its left change?

materials.item: your home's electricity meter, or the kilometre counter (odometer) of a scooter, car or auto
a notebook and a pencil

projects.safety: Only look at the electricity meter. Do not touch it or the wires near it. A grown-up comes with you each time.

schedule.what: Read the meter and copy every digit into a place value chart.
Read it again. Circle the digits that changed. Predict tomorrow's reading.
Read it again and check your prediction.
Read it again. Work out how much was used in three days.
Last reading. Say when the next digit to the left will change.

projects.record: Draw a place value chart with one row for each day. Write the reading in it at the same time each day. Circle every digit that changed since the day before.

setup.art: A home electricity meter on a wall showing a row of digits, with a child and a grown-up looking at it from a step away.
setup.caption: 1. Read the row of digits on the meter. Do not touch it.

setup.art: A notebook with a place value chart and five rows of meter readings, with the changed digits circled.
setup.caption: 2. Write the reading in a chart each day. Circle what changed.

setup.art: A close view of a scooter's kilometre counter showing 09,999 about to roll over to 10,000.
setup.caption: 3. Watch for the moment a 9 rolls over and the digit on its left goes up by one.

flow.do: 1. Go to the meter together. 2. Your child reads the digits aloud from left to right. 3. Your child copies them into a place value chart.
flow.say: Read me the digits on the meter. Which place is each one in? Which digit do you think will change first?
flow.kid: Read the digits on the meter. Write them in a place value chart. Which digit will change first?

ask.q: Which digit will change first, and why?
good: The one on the right, because it counts ones.
The ones digit.

flow.parent: An electricity meter counts units of electricity. An odometer counts kilometres. Some meters show a digit after a decimal point in a different colour. Leave that digit out.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Meter Watch, a five-day project where you read a meter that counts in places. You take the first reading.

flow.do: 1. On days 2, 3 and 4, read the meter at the same time of day. 2. Your child circles the digits that changed. 3. Your child subtracts to find what was used, and predicts the next reading.
flow.say: Which digits changed since yesterday? How much was used? What do you think it will say tomorrow?
flow.kid: Read the meter each day. Circle the digits that changed. Guess what it will say tomorrow.
flow.wait: Do this on each of the next three days.

ask.q: Why does the right-hand digit change most?
good: It counts ones, and ones are used up fastest.
The next digit only moves when ten ones are full.

flow.context: These are days 2 to 4 of Meter Watch, a five-day project where you read a meter that counts in places. You read the meter each day and predict the next reading.

flow.do: 1. Take the last reading. 2. Your child finds the total used in the four days. 3. Ask when the digit in the next place to the left will go up.
flow.say: Look at the tens digit, or the hundreds digit. How many more units before it goes up by one?
flow.kid: Take the last reading. How much was used in all? When will the next digit to the left go up?

ask.q: The meter shows 4,297. How many more units until the hundreds digit changes?
good: 3 more. Then it shows 4,300.

check.q: A kilometre counter shows 09,999. What does it show after one more kilometre?
check.why: One more makes ten in the ones place. That ten is passed to the tens, which passes ten on to the hundreds, and so on. Every 9 rolls to 0 and a 1 appears in the ten thousands place.

flow.context: This is day 5 of Meter Watch, a five-day project where you read a meter that counts in places. You take the last reading and work out when the next place will change.

challenges.title: Stretch: send any number up to 31 with one hand
challenges.context: This is a design challenge that goes past Class 5. You must show any number from 0 to 31 using only the five fingers of one hand, each finger either up or down.
challenges.problem: Your friend is across the room and you may not speak. You have one hand. Each finger is either up or down. Find a way to send her any number from 0 to 31.
constraints: You may use only one hand, and each finger must be clearly up or clearly down.
You may hold up your hand only once for each number. No showing 5 and then 5 again.
Your friend must be able to work out the number with no other hints.
materials: 5 slips of paper and a pencil
general: Hold up one finger for each one. This is how most people show numbers, but it stops at 5.
Flash the hand several times and add up the fingers. This reaches 31, but it breaks the rule of showing the hand only once.
Use two hands. This reaches 10, but the problem gives you one hand.
creative: Give each finger its own value: 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16. Each value is two times the one before. Add the values of the fingers that are up.
Label five cups 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. A cup is either full with exactly that many beans or empty. Every heap from 0 to 31 beans fits in exactly one way.
Write down which cups are full as 1 and which are empty as 0. For 22 beans you get 10110. This is base two, the way a computer writes numbers.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own code. Try places worth 1, 3 and 9, where each finger can be down, half up or fully up. What is the biggest number three fingers can send? Test your code on someone at home.

setup.art: Five katoris in a row with paper labels 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1, and a heap of 22 beans beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Label five cups 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. Take a heap of beans.

setup.art: The same cups with 16 beans in the first, none in the second, 4 in the third, 2 in the fourth and none in the last.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the biggest cup you can, then the next. A cup is full or empty.

setup.art: A child's hand with the thumb up, the first finger up, the middle and ring fingers folded down and the little finger up, next to the written code 11001 and the number 25.
setup.caption: 3. Fingers up for full cups. Your hand now shows the number.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem aloud. 2. Let your child try for three minutes with no help. 3. Ask how far their way can count.
flow.say: Show me any number up to 31 with one hand, held up once. Try your own ideas first.
flow.kid: Try to show any number up to 31 with one hand. Hold it up only once. How far can you get?

ask.q: What is the biggest number your way can show?
good: Only 5.
I ran out of fingers.

flow.parent: Most children get to 5 and stop. That is the right place to be stuck. Do not give the answer yet.
flow.context: This is the first step of the five-finger challenge, where you send any number up to 31 with one hand. You try your own ideas first.

flow.do: 1. Label the five cups 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. 2. Give your child 22 beans. 3. The rule: a cup must hold exactly its number of beans, or nothing. 4. Start with the biggest cup that can be filled.
flow.say: Each cup must be full or empty. Start with the biggest cup you can fill. Which cups end up full?
flow.kid: Put 22 beans into the cups. A cup is full or empty. Start with the biggest cup you can fill.

ask.q: Which cups are full for 22 beans?
good: Sixteen, four and two. 16 + 4 + 2 = 22.

check.q: The cups 16, 4 and 1 are full. The cups 8 and 2 are empty. How many beans is that?
check.why: Add the full cups: 16 + 4 + 1 = 21. Picking 3 counts the cups, when each cup has its own value.

flow.context: This is step 2 of the five-finger challenge, where you send any number up to 31 with one hand. You sort 22 beans into cups worth 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.

flow.do: 1. Now each finger stands for a cup: thumb 16, then 8, 4, 2, and little finger 1. 2. Your child shows 25 with fingers. 3. Take turns sending and reading numbers across the room.
flow.say: Your thumb is the 16 cup and your little finger is the 1 cup. Show me 25. Now send me a secret number.
flow.kid: Each finger is a cup. Thumb is 16. Little finger is 1. Show 25. Then send a secret number.

ask.q: Which fingers are up for 25?
good: Thumb, first finger and little finger.

ask.q: All five fingers are up. What number is that?

flow.parent: Some finger shapes are hard to hold. Your child can use the other hand to keep a finger down.
flow.context: This is step 3 of the five-finger challenge, where you send any number up to 31 with one hand. You use fingers as places worth 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1.

flow.do: 1. Ask how the finger values are like lakhs, thousands and ones, and how they differ. 2. Read 'Your turn' aloud. 3. Your child invents a code and tests it on you.
flow.say: In our numbers each place is ten times the one before. What is each finger place worth compared with the one before?
flow.kid: Our places go up ten times each. How do the finger places go up? Now invent your own code.

ask.q: How do the finger places go up?
good: Two times each: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16.
They double.

flow.parent: With places worth 1, 3 and 9 and three positions for each finger, the biggest number is 2 + 6 + 18 = 26.
flow.context: This is the last step of the five-finger challenge, where you send any number up to 31 with one hand. You compare your finger code with ordinary place value and invent a new code.

worksheets.title: Read It, Write It, Place It (core)

items.p: Write in figures, with Indian commas: three lakh forty-five thousand six hundred.
items.why: Go period by period: 3 in the lakhs, 45 in the thousands, 600 in the ones. That gives 3,45,600.

items.p: In 4,72,518, what is the value of the digit 7?
items.why: The 7 stands in the ten thousands place, so it is worth 70,000. Picking 7 gives the face value, not the place value.

items.p: One lakh is a 1 followed by ____ zeros.
items.why: One lakh is 1,00,000. Count the zeros: there are five.

items.p: In 5,05,050 every 5 has the same value.
items.why: False. From the left, the three 5s are worth 5,00,000, then 5,000, then 50. The place gives each one its value.

items.p: Match each place to what a 1 in that place is worth.
items.why: Each place is ten times the place on its right: 100, then 1,000, then 10,000, then 1,00,000.

items.p: Put these places in order, from the smallest value to the biggest.
items.why: The places go up from right to left. Each one is ten times the one before.
The 6 stands in the thousands place, so it is worth 6,000.

items.p: Which number is four lakh seven thousand nine?
items.why: 4 lakhs, no ten thousands, 7 thousands, no hundreds, no tens, 9 ones: 4,07,009. Picking 47,009 leaves out the zero that holds the ten thousands place.
4 lakhs, 2 ten thousands and 5 ones. Zeros hold the thousands, hundreds and tens: 4,20,005.

items.p: 1,00,000 and 100,000 are the same number.
items.why: True. Both are a 1 followed by five zeros. The first has Indian commas and the second has international commas.

items.p: Look at the commas. Sort each number: Indian system or international system?
items.why: From the right, the Indian system has three digits and then groups of two. The international system has groups of three all the way.

items.p: How many thousands make one lakh?
items.why: One lakh is 1,00,000, and 1,00,000 ÷ 1,000 = 100. Picking 10 gives ten thousand, which is one place short.

items.p: Draw a place value chart from lakhs to ones. Write 7,31,406 in it.
items.a: Six columns named Lakhs, Ten thousands, Thousands, Hundreds, Tens and Ones, holding 7, 3, 1, 4, 0 and 6.
items.why: A strong chart has one digit in each column, with the zero written in the tens column and not left blank.

items.p: Explain why a 6 in the lakhs place is worth ten times a 6 in the ten thousands place.
items.a: Because ten ten-thousands make one lakh. So 6 lakhs is the same as 60 ten-thousands, which is ten times 6 ten-thousands.
items.why: A strong answer uses the exchange: ten of one place make one of the next place to the left.

items.p: Write 5,06,070 in words. Then say what each zero is doing.
items.a: Five lakh six thousand seventy. The zeros hold the ten thousands, hundreds and ones places, which are empty.
items.why: A strong answer names the three empty places. Without the zeros the digits 5, 6 and 7 would slide together into 567.

items.p: Draw a number line from 0 to 1,00,000 with a mark at every 10,000. Mark 50,000 and 75,000.
items.a: Ten equal gaps. 50,000 is on the fifth mark, exactly half way. 75,000 is half way between the seventh and eighth marks.
items.why: A strong line has equal gaps, because each gap stands for the same amount, 10,000.

items.p: Write 250,000 with Indian commas.
items.why: Take out the comma: 250000. From the right, count three digits and then two: 2,50,000. It is two lakh fifty thousand.

items.p: Which is the same as one million?
items.why: One million is 1,000,000, a 1 with six zeros. Ten lakh is 10,00,000, also a 1 with six zeros. 100 lakh is one crore.

items.p: 7 lakh = ____ thousand.
items.why: One lakh is 100 thousand. So 7 lakh is 7 × 100 = 700 thousand.

items.p: Match each Indian name to its international name.
items.why: One lakh is 100 thousand, and ten lakh make one million. So 30 lakh is 3 million.
Every digit moves one place to the left, and a zero holds the empty ones place: 47,250.

items.p: When you multiply a whole number by 100, each digit moves:
items.why: Multiplying by 100 makes each digit worth a hundred times as much, which is two places to the left. Moving right is what dividing does.
Dividing by 1,000 moves every digit three places to the right. 3,60,000 becomes 360.
False. Every digit moves one place to the left, so 2.5 × 10 = 25. Writing a zero after 2.5 gives 2.50, which is still two and a half.

items.p: Put these in order, from the smallest to the biggest.
items.why: In figures they are 99,999, then 1,00,000, then 9,99,999, then 10,00,000, then 10,10,000.

items.p: A video has 1.2M views. How many views is that?
items.why: M means million. 1.2 million is 1,200,000, which is 12,00,000 or twelve lakh. Picking 1,20,000 reads M as lakh.

items.p: Sort each amount: bigger than one lakh, or smaller than one lakh?
items.why: One lakh is 100 thousand. 250K is 250 thousand and half a million is 500 thousand, so both are bigger. 9 × 10,000 is 90,000, which is smaller.

items.p: The number just before 10,00,000 is ____.
items.why: Take one away from ten lakh. Every place rolls back to 9: 9,99,999.

items.p: A cheque says 1,200,000 rupees. Write it with Indian commas and in words. Explain what you did.
items.a: 12,00,000, twelve lakh rupees. I took out the commas and put them back the Indian way: after three digits from the right, then after every two.
items.why: A strong answer says that no digit moved. Only the commas changed.

items.p: Two newspapers print the same price for a flat: ₹45,00,000 and ₹4,500,000.

views.says: 45 lakh is clearer. I think in lakhs.
4.5 million is clearer. I think in millions.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then says both prices are the same number, and each way is clear to the people who grew up with it.
items.why: Neither way is more correct. The digits and their places are the same. The grouping is a habit that each reader learnt.

items.p: Draw two place value charts. Show the digits of 3,405 moving when you multiply by 10.
items.a: 3,405 in the top chart and 34,050 in the bottom chart, with an arrow from each digit to the column on its left and a zero in the ones column.
items.why: A strong drawing shows every digit moving one column to the left, with the zero filling the empty ones place.

items.p: How many ₹100 notes make ₹1,00,000?
items.why: 1,00,000 ÷ 100 = 1,000. Every digit moves two places to the right.

items.p: Use the digits 7, 0, 3, 9, 1, 5 once each. Write the biggest 6-digit number.
items.why: Put the biggest digit in the biggest place, then the next biggest: 9, 7, 5, 3, 1, 0.

items.p: Use the digits 7, 0, 3, 9, 1, 5 once each. Write the smallest 6-digit number.
items.why: The smallest digit, 0, can not go first, or the number would have only five digits. So 1 goes first, then 0, then the rest in order.

items.p: How many times bigger is the 4 in 4,00,000 than the 4 in 400?
items.why: The 4 has moved three places to the left. Each place is ten times, so 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000 times. Check: 400 × 1,000 = 4,00,000.

items.p: A digit is worth 100 times the same digit two places to its right.
items.why: True. One place to the left is ten times, so two places is 10 × 10 = 100 times. The 3 in 300 is 100 times the 3 in 3.

items.p: How many 6-digit numbers are there in all?
items.why: They run from 1,00,000 to 9,99,999. Take the 99,999 smaller numbers away from 9,99,999 and 9,00,000 are left.
One less than one lakh. Every zero rolls back to 9, and the lakhs place becomes empty: 99,999.

items.p: Put these amounts in order, smallest first.
items.why: In figures they are 3,500, then 35,000, then 3,50,000, then 20,00,000, then 25,00,000.

items.p: Match each sum to its answer.
items.why: Multiplying moves the digits 4 and 8 to the left, and dividing moves them to the right. Count the places each time.

items.p: In base two the places are worth 16, 8, 4, 2 and 1. What number is 10110 in base two?
items.why: The 1s stand in the 16, 4 and 2 places. 16 + 4 + 2 = 22.

items.p: The Japanese word 'man' means 10,000. How many man make one lakh?
items.why: One lakh is ten ten-thousands, so it is 10 man. Japan groups big numbers by ten-thousands, where India groups by lakhs.

items.p: Sort each one: chosen by people, or true whatever people choose?
items: Ten heaps of ten thousand make a heap of a lakh
A heap of 12 beans has more than a heap of 9
items.why: Names, signs, commas and the base are agreements. How many things are in a heap does not depend on what anyone calls it.

items.p: Every 6-digit whole number is bigger than every 5-digit whole number.
items.why: True. The smallest 6-digit number is 1,00,000, and the biggest 5-digit number is 99,999, which is one less.

items.p: Convince a friend that 10 lakh and 1 million are the same number. Use a place value chart.
items.a: Both are a 1 with six zeros. In the chart the 1 stands in the seventh place from the right both times. Only the commas and the name differ.
items.why: A strong answer writes both numbers in one chart, digit by digit, and shows that they match.

items.p: Imagine numbers with a new sign for every bigger size, and no zero. What goes wrong with very big numbers?
items.a: Every bigger size needs a new sign, so the signs never end. Sums are also slow, because the signs do not line up in places.
items.why: A strong answer sees that place value needs only ten signs for any size, because the place does the work that new signs did.

items.p: Is '1,00,000 = 100,000' a fact about the world or an agreement between people?

views.says: It is an agreement. People could put the commas anywhere.
It is a fact. A lakh of grains is the same heap, whatever you call it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, then grants the other side its point: the commas and names are agreed, and the amount is not.
items.why: Both girls are right about a different part. The writing is chosen. The amount it stands for is not.

items.p: In base five, five ones make one 'five'. Draw 13 beans grouped this way, and write the number in base five.
items.a: Two groups of five beans and three single beans, written 23 in base five.
items.why: 13 is two fives and three ones. In base five the left place counts fives, so the number is written 23.

items.p: A bank packet has 100 notes. How many packets of ₹500 notes make ₹10,00,000?
items.why: One packet is 100 × 500 = ₹50,000. Two packets make one lakh, so ten lakh need 20 packets.

quiz.p: Which is five lakh six thousand twenty, in figures?
quiz.why: 5 lakhs, no ten thousands, 6 thousands, no hundreds, 2 tens, no ones: 5,06,020. Picking 56,020 drops the zero that holds the ten thousands place.

quiz.p: Write in figures: nine lakh nine.
quiz.why: 9 in the lakhs place and 9 in the ones place. Four zeros hold the empty places between them.

quiz.p: How do you read 640,000 in the international system?
quiz.why: The thousands period says 640, so it is six hundred forty thousand. In the Indian system the same number is six lakh forty thousand.

quiz.p: In 8,35,271, what is the value of the 3?
quiz.why: The 3 stands in the ten thousands place, so it is worth 30,000. Picking 3 gives the face value.

quiz.p: Each place is worth ten times the place on its right.
quiz.why: True. Ten ones make a ten, ten tens make a hundred, and so on up to lakhs and beyond.

quiz.p: The 6 in 6,00,000 is how many times the 6 in 60,000?
quiz.why: The lakhs place is one place to the left of the ten thousands place, so it is worth ten times as much.
3 lakhs, 4 thousands and 5 tens. Zeros hold the ten thousands, hundreds and ones: 3,04,050.

quiz.p: What does the zero do in 4,05,312?
opts: It holds the ten thousands place.
It makes the number ten times bigger.
quiz.why: The zero shows there are no ten thousands and keeps the 4 in the lakhs place. Drop it and the number becomes 45,312.
Every digit moves two places to the left, and zeros hold the tens and ones: 2,34,000.
Dividing by 10 moves every digit one place to the right: 5,600. Picking 5,60,000 moves the digits the wrong way.

quiz.p: How many lakh make one million?
quiz.why: One million is 10,00,000, which is ten lakh. A hundred lakh make one crore.

quiz.p: Which shows twelve lakh with international commas?
quiz.why: Twelve lakh has seven digits: 1200000. With a comma after every three digits from the right it is 1,200,000.
False. Both have the digits 2, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0 in the same places. Only the commas differ.

quiz.p: Which of these did people choose, and could have chosen differently?
opts: How many grains are in a heap
quiz.why: Commas, names and the base are agreements. The amount in a heap does not change with what we call it.

quiz.p: People in Japan group big numbers by ten-thousands. What does this show?
opts: Grouping is a choice people make
Ten thousand is bigger in Japan
quiz.why: The numbers are the same everywhere. Different peoples chose different ways to group and name them.

applications: A bank clerk reads the amount on a cheque in figures and in words, and both must match. One misplaced digit changes the amount ten times over.
The census counts the people of every town and village. Town populations are reported in thousands and lakhs.
A newspaper prints the price of a flat as ₹45 lakh. A website for buyers abroad prints the same price as 4.5 million rupees.
An electricity meter and a vehicle's kilometre counter are rows of digit wheels. Each wheel passes one on to the wheel on its left after every ten.
Scientists write the distance to the Moon, about 3,84,400 km, in the international way so that readers in every country group it alike.
A computer stores every number in places worth 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on. It is place value with two digits where we use ten.
A shopkeeper in a wholesale market works out 1,000 bags at ₹250 each by moving digits: ₹2,50,000.
A cricket board reports that a stadium holds 50,000 people. Two full houses are one lakh tickets.

open_questions.q: Does every digit turn up equally often in the endless digits of the number pi?
open_questions.why_open: Pi is the number you get when you divide the distance round a circle by the distance across it. Its digits go on for ever. Computers have checked trillions of them, and each digit from 0 to 9 turns up about one time in ten. Nobody has been able to prove that this goes on for ever.

open_questions.q: Why did people settle on counting in tens?
open_questions.why_open: The likely reason is our ten fingers. But nobody wrote the reason down, and other peoples chose twenty and sixty. It may never be possible to prove.

open_questions.q: How does a desert ant keep track of thousands of steps?
open_questions.why_open: The 2006 experiment showed that ants measure distance by their steps. How the ant's body and brain add the steps up has not been found.

open_questions.q: Does a honeybee understand zero the way we do?
open_questions.why_open: Bees placed a blank card below one. Whether that is the same idea as our zero, or something of the bees' own, is still argued about.

maths.problem: Suppose your one lakh grains of rice weighed 2 kg. About how many grains are in a 10 kg bag of the same rice?
maths.explain: 10 kg is five lots of 2 kg. Each lot holds about one lakh grains. So the bag holds about 5 × 1,00,000 = 5,00,000 grains.
maths.context: In the Rice Test you built one lakh grains of rice in a pot. This problem uses your pot to work out a number nobody could count.
maths.why_maths: Nobody can count the grains in a bag. Once you know what one lakh grains weigh, multiplying gives you the answer.

maths.problem: You found that 1,000 mm is 1 metre and that 1,00,000 mm is 100 metres. How many kilometres is 10,00,000 mm?
maths.explain: 10,00,000 mm is ten times 1,00,000 mm. Ten times 100 metres is 1,000 metres, and 1,000 metres is 1 kilometre. So one million millimetres make one kilometre.
maths.context: In A Lakh on a String you made each length ten times the one before. This problem takes one more step of ten.
maths.why_maths: Units of length go up in tens, like places. Moving the digits changes millimetres to metres to kilometres without long sums.

maths.problem: Count your heartbeats for one minute. Use that number to work out about how many times your heart beats in a day. Is it more or less than one lakh?
maths.answer: At 70 beats a minute it is 1,00,800 beats a day, just over one lakh. At 90 beats a minute it is 1,29,600.
maths.explain: A day has 60 × 24 = 1,440 minutes. At 70 beats a minute, 70 × 1,440 = 1,00,800. A child's heart often beats faster than 70, so your answer may be nearer one and a half lakh.
maths.context: In the Rice Test you saw how big one lakh is. This problem looks for a lakh inside your own body.
maths.why_maths: Your heart never stops, so nobody can count a day of beats. Counting one minute and multiplying gives a good answer.

maths.problem: In the game Place It you turn over 3, 8, 0, 5, 9 and 1. What is the biggest number you could have made? What is the smallest 6-digit number? How far apart are they?
maths.explain: For the biggest number put the digits in order from big to small: 9,85,310. For the smallest put them from small to big, but 0 can not go first, so start with 1: 1,03,589. Subtract: 9,85,310 − 1,03,589 = 8,81,721. The same six digits give numbers nearly nine lakh apart.
maths.context: In the game Place It you chose a place for each digit as it was turned over. This problem asks what the best and the worst choices would have been.
maths.why_maths: It shows how much the place matters. The digits are the same, and only where they stand differs.

maths.problem: A shopkeeper has ₹1,00,000 in ₹200 notes. How many notes is that? Use what you found for ₹100 notes.
maths.explain: One lakh rupees is 1,000 notes of ₹100. A ₹200 note is worth two ₹100 notes, so half as many notes are needed: 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500.
maths.context: In Bundles at the Bank you found how many ₹100 notes make one lakh rupees. This problem changes the note.
maths.why_maths: A fact you already know, worked from place value, saves you from a long division.

maths.problem: Light travels about 3,00,000 km in one second. The Moon is about 3,84,400 km away. Does moonlight take more or less than one second to reach you? Explain without dividing.
maths.answer: A little more than one second.
maths.explain: Compare the two numbers place by place. Both have 3 in the lakhs place. In the ten thousands place the Moon's distance has 8 and light's distance in a second has 0. So the Moon is farther than light goes in one second. It is less than twice as far, so the time is between one and two seconds. It is about 1.3 seconds.
maths.context: In A Lakh on a String you saw that one lakh millimetres is only 100 metres. This problem uses lakhs of kilometres, the distances of space.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two big numbers place by place tells you which is bigger without doing any sum.

roots.context: We have been reading lakhs and millions and moving digits from place to place. Now we ask what place value tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Write a 5 on paper. Is it five rupees or five lakh rupees? You cannot tell. A digit is worth what its place says. The 5 in 50 and the 5 in 5,00,000 are the same mark.
deep_truth.habit: We think a number's value sits inside the digit, like in a ₹5 coin. It does not. It comes from where the digit stands. 'Lakh' and 'million' are names people chose for groups of zeros.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Rice Test, one spoon held a thousand grains and one tumbler ten thousand. In Two Commas, One Number, 12,00,000 and 1,200,000 had the same digits. Only the commas moved.

three.who_am_i: A digit is worth what its place makes it. You also stand in many places: a daughter at home, a pupil in class, a bowler on the field. You are the same person in each, and each place asks something different of you.
three.what_is_life: Honeybees place nothing below one. Desert ants keep track of how far they have walked. Keeping count is something many living beings do. Writing the count down in places is the human way of doing it.
three.what_is_this_world: The world has heaps, distances and crowds. It has no commas and no lakhs. Those are ours. But ten potfuls of a lakh grains make the same heap, whatever anyone calls it.

roots.thread: Every number is built from ten signs: 0 to 9. Zero holds a place that is empty. A 1 that moves one place to the left becomes ten, then a hundred, then a lakh. So ten signs are enough to write a number of any size.

teachings.teaching: Aryabhata names ten places in order, from one to a hundred crore, and then says that from place to place each is ten times the one before.
teachings.link: This is the rule you found with rice. One line, written in 499 CE, covers every place there is and every place anyone will ever add.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at the hub of a wheel, but the wheel is useful because of the empty hole at the centre. A pot is made of clay, but it is useful because of the empty space inside.
teachings.link: Zero is the empty space of our number system. It is worth nothing, yet without it 4,05,000 could not be told from 45.

teachings.teaching: The Buddhist teacher Nagarjuna says that whatever arises depending on other things is empty of a nature of its own.
teachings.link: A digit is like this. A 5 has no fixed worth of its own. It is worth five lakh, or fifty, depending on the digits that stand around it.

science.text: People in Japan and China group big numbers by ten-thousands. People in India group them by lakhs and crores. English speakers group them by thousands and millions. All of them write the same numbers.
People probably count in tens because we have ten fingers. Nobody can prove this, and other peoples have counted in twenties and in sixties.

other_view.who: G. H. Hardy, an English mathematician, in his book A Mathematician's Apology (1940)
other_view.view: Hardy held that numbers are real in their own right, apart from people. He wrote that 317 is a prime number 'not because we think so', but because mathematical reality is built that way. On this view the commas and the names are only clothing. The number underneath was never chosen by anyone.

practice.title: From one grain to a lakh and back
practice.say: Sit still and close your eyes. Picture one grain of rice on your palm. Now picture ten grains in a row. Now ten rows, a small square of a hundred. Now a spoonful, a thousand. Now a tumbler, and now a full pot, one lakh. Breathe in slowly. Now go back down: the pot, the tumbler, the spoon, the square, the row, the one grain. Open your eyes. Was the one grain still there inside the lakh?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Picture one grain of rice. Now ten in a row. Now a hundred in a square. Now a spoonful, then a tumbler, then a pot. Now go back down to one grain. Was the one grain inside the pot all along?

ask: Is the value of a digit in the digit, in its place, or in the person who reads it?
If everyone in the world forgot the word 'lakh' tonight, would there still be a lakh of grains in the pot?
Zero is worth nothing, yet it changes every digit on its left. What else in your life matters by being empty?
People chose to count in tens. What else do you take as fixed that somebody once chose?

how_we_found_out.context: Who worked out that ten signs are enough to write any number? This card tells what is known, and what is not.
how_we_found_out.story: In ancient Egypt, scribes wrote numbers with a different sign for each size. A stroke meant 1, a coil of rope meant 100, and a tadpole meant 1,00,000. For a bigger size they needed one more new sign. Many peoples wrote numbers in this way, and it seemed that bigger numbers must always need more signs. Mathematicians in India showed that this is not so. They let the place of a digit give its size, and they used a sign for an empty place. With that, nine digits and a zero can write any whole number at all. We do not know the names of the people who first did this. In 499 CE Aryabhata, who was 23, listed the names of ten places, from one up to a hundred crore, and wrote that each place is ten times the one before. In 628 CE Brahmagupta wrote down rules for doing sums with zero. A temple inscription at Gwalior, cut in 876 CE, shows the number 270 with a zero, written the way we write it today.
how_we_found_out.who: Unnamed Indian mathematicians, and later Aryabhata and Brahmagupta
how_we_found_out.when: Place value was in use in India by about 500 CE. Aryabhata wrote in 499 CE and Brahmagupta in 628 CE.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Bigger numbers must need more and more new signs. Place value with zero showed that ten signs are enough for every number, however big.

playtest: Walked through every flow as a parent and one child in a flat. The Rice Test needs about 2.5 kg of rice, which goes back in the tin. Walk Like a Desert Ant needs about 6 metres of clear floor with the cushion in the middle, because the giant steps carry the child past it. Counting the first thousand grains is the slow part and takes two people about eight minutes. After that the amounts are measured, not counted, so one lakh is close and not exact. The table of sample results is an estimate worked out from grain weights, not a test done in a kitchen: a thousand grains should come to about a tablespoon and a lakh to between 1 and 2.5 kg, but your rice may differ. If you have less rice, stop at three tumblers and work out the rest. Place It was played in the head with 1, 2 and 3 players: six turns each, 18 of the 20 cards at most, and nobody can get stuck. Lakh and Million Pairs has 24 cards written out in full. Every pair was checked digit by digit. In the five-finger challenge some finger shapes are hard to hold. Use the other hand to hold a finger down. Every answer in the worksheets, quiz and maths problems was worked out again by a script. Step minutes add up to each activity's minutes.
